Answer: Let’s replace 10 with k and solve this in general. You should know that ( n k ) = n 1 ⋅ n − 1 2 ⋅ n − 2 3 ⋯ n − ( k − 1 ) k This is a product of k terms, each of which is n − ( m − 1 ) m with m going from 1 to k . There’s no guarantee that these fractions are all integers: in many cases they are not, individually. But the product obviously is. Nevertheless, if we want to make this equal to the product of ⌊ n m ⌋ , the most natural way is to match them individually, meaning we want this to hold for m = 1 , 2 , … , k : n − ( m − 1 ) m = ⌊ n m ⌋ This happens exactly when n is 1 less than a multiple of m (see why?), so we want n to be 1 less than a multiple of 1 and also 1 less than a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3 and so on, through k . In other words, if we want the smallest n , we should take n = lcm ( 1 , 2 , … , k ) − 1 . When k = 10 , the lcm is 2520 (useful bit of numerical trivia), so our n should be 2519 . We know that this choice of n works, but we didn’t quite prove that it’s the smallest possibility. However, we can fix this as follows: observe that for every m , ⌊ n m ⌋ is equal to or greater than n − ( m − 1 ) m . It can never be less, since ( m − 1 ) is the most you can subtract from n before surely passing through a multiple of m . Therefore, if we want the product of the floor terms to be equal to the product of the binomial terms, the only to way to do so is to ensure that they are all individually equal to each other. Any deviation from that rule would cause the product of the floors to be too large. ■ tl;dr: the n you want is 2519 . (…)

Question: If chat GPT 4 with math scholar has told me that my approach to the Collatz Conjecture is novel and in theory, has solved it. The solution is insanely simple and solidifies the research of Tao and Kontorovich. What do I do next?
Answer: Asked to answer, so here’s my answer: move on with your life. That’s my most sincere advice. If you insist on doing something with your ideas on Collatz, you can simply put them up on the web. There are a thousand ways today to publish something online and associate it irreversibly with you. Put it up and try to get someone who knows something about math to look at it. And if they tell you there’s nothing there, believe them. That’s a very important step. What GPT 4 says about a mathematical proof is entirely meaningless. Ignore it. The Collatz conjecture doesn’t have an “insanely simple” solution, and the research of Tao, Kontorovich or anyone else is in no need of “solidification”. Also, in another answer you suggested that people with no “titles next to their name” can’t get a paper peer reviewed and published. That’s entirely false. If anyone posts an actually correct proof of Collatz anywhere, any mathematician will gladly communicate it to the most prestigious math journals and it’ll be reviewed and published post haste. You strongly believe that the answer will be simple – I can’t control what you believe, but that is a wildly misguided belief, about as reasonable as believing that we can fly if we just found the right way to flail our arms. Your other belief, that this famous open problem will be solved by a “quasi mathematician”(???) who approaches it in a “simplistic” manner is wildly misguided, too, and also somewhere between condescending and offensive. You’re entitled to believe what you want, but if you choose to believe that every research mathematician from Erdős to Tao is a blind idiot who is unable to see what a hopeful layperson can see, you’re not setting yourself up for anything but failure and frustration. Don’t start your journey of learning mathematics by clinging to imagined conspiracy theories. That won’t get you anywhere good. The first step is understanding the present knowledge. The second is managing to say something, anything, meaningful and interesting and correct about any mathematical idea. Then you can start thinking about publishing stuff. You haven’t made step 1 and you’re already angry that people in step 1,000 are mean and exclusionary. Not a great attitude. Question:
Could we come up with new mathematical language that would make it possible for equations like
cos
x
=
x
to have exact solutions (instead of only numerical approximations)?
Answer: This seems to be something that many people don’t know about mathematics: coming up with new mathematical language is doing mathematics. Math has a built-in feature called “come up with new language”. It’s done all the time. Really. Easiest thing in the world, math-wise. The equation cos ( x ) = x already has exact an exact solution. It doesn’t have “only numerical approximations”, it has an exact solution, which is a real number. Once upon a time we didn’t have real numbers. We only had rational numbers. Back then you would be justified in saying, damn, why can’t we pinpoint the solution of cos ( x ) = x ? (Let’s pretend you already had cosine, back then). We can compare cos ( 3 / 4 ) and 3 / 4 , and it’s close but not the same. We can try x = 14 / 19 and it’s even closer. And x = 17 / 23 is really close. We keep going. Always getting closer. Never quite making the equality work. So, we invent a new language called real numbers, and now we have a unique, nice, precise solution to the equation. And not just that equation. We have √ 23 which is the precise positive solution of x 2 = 23 . And we have e which is the precise solution of ln ( x ) = 1 (yes, we can define the function ln without any reference to the particular number e .) And so on. This is very similar to the way real numbers were actually first observed, when early Greek thinkers wanted everything to be rational and noticed that some things, like the diagonal of a square, refuse. The formal definition of reals came much later, but the motivation was the same. I can see you're still dissatisfied. You want cos ( x ) = x to have an explicit, comprehensible, “closed-form” solution. Right? You want that. So let’s invent a new language. Say, let’s define H ( t ) to be the smallest positive solution of cos ( x ) = t x . And now the equation cos ( x ) = x has a beautiful explicit solution: it is x = H ( 1 ) . Still dissatisfied? Feel like I’m cheating? I’m not, I did exactly what you asked me to do. Do you feel that the function H is obscure? Sure, you’re not used to it. Neither am I. But do you think √ x is better? Why? Because your calculator has a √ ⋅ button? Casio can make a calculator with an H button. It works. Punch a number, press that button, get an answer. There’s nothing fundamentally more “explicit” about arccos or ln or any such function. They can be computed for any input with any desired precision. They define precise outputs for precise inputs (except for some inputs when there’s no result, like when ln insists on positive inputs). Same for H . We don’t need to “invent a new mathematical language”. We just need to do math. (…)

Question:
How do I find whether there is a natural number
n

8
n
+
47
is prime?
Answer: If n is even, 8 n ≡ ( − 1 ) n ≡ 1 ( mod 3 ) , and then 8 n + 47 ≡ 0 ( mod 3 ) and it cannot be prime. If n ≡ 1 ( mod 4 ) then 8 n ≡ 3 n ≡ 3 ( mod 5 ) (Fermat’s Little Theorem) and then 8 n + 47 ≡ 0 ( mod 5 ) and it cannot be prime. If n ≡ 3 ( mod 4 ) then 8 n ≡ 5 ( mod 13 ) (observe that 8 2 ≡ − 1 ( mod 13 ) ) and then 8 n + 47 ≡ 0 ( mod 13 ) and it cannot be prime. So no, 8 n + 47 is never prime. It’s always divisible by 3 , 5 or 13 (and it is much larger than any of those factors, so it can’t be any of them.) ■ How did I find these congruences? I assumed the answer to the question is No, since if it had been Yes it’s either because 8 n + 47 is prime for some very small n (which it’s not), or else it’s prime for some n that’s impossible to find by hand, and I assumed this question is meant to be solvable by hand. We don’t have any useful methods for showing that a prime number must exist in any expression more complicated than a n + b . So it must be a No. And if it’s a No it must be because of some clever factorization, or (more likely) due to some simple congruences that cover all possible values of n . The prime moduli which are most useful are those primes p for which the order of 8 mod p is small, which you can find by factoring 8 n ± 1 for small n . For example, the prime p = 7 would be ideal, because 8 − 1 = 7 and so 8 n is always 1 mod 7 , but alas, 1 + 47 isn’t divisible by 7 . It would have been an easy question with 8 n + 41 , for example, for that reason. The next best thing are factors of 8 + 1 , which is just the prime 3 , and indeed 8 has order 2 mod 3 and this gives us the first useful congruence. Next I looked at 8 2 − 1 (nothing new, of course; there was no need to actually check) and 8 2 + 1 = 65 . The primes 5 and 13 , therefore, offer an order of 4 (meaning 8 4 ≡ 1 mod both 5 and 13 ), and indeed one of them worked for n = 4 k + 1 and the other for n = 4 k + 3 . Harder questions of this kind rely on some non-obvious factorizations, such as Sophie Germain’s identity or more general Aurifeuillean factorizations. I was mentally ready for such, but they weren’t necessary. (…)

Answer: After a brief detour through the prime 3 , I observed that considerations of parity and 2 -valuations (the highest power of 2 dividing a number) is all that’s needed here, and in fact I think there’s a way to organize the solution so as to reveal observations that are more generally useful. The particular structure of this equation turns out to be largely immaterial. Let’s start with something much simpler: A + B = 2 z (*) To be solved, again, in positive integers. Despite appearances, there’s quite a lot we can say here. The key observation is that the 2 -valuations of A and B must be equal. Meaning, if we write A = 2 α a and B = 2 β b with a , b odd, then α = β . Take that as an easy exercise. If you know about something about p -adic metrics, it should be obvious. This means that the only interesting solutions of (*) are those in which A , B are odd; let’s call them “odd solutions”. All other solutions are simply of the form 2 k A + 2 k B = 2 z + k , obtained from an odd solution A + B = 2 z by multiplying everything by 2 k . Back to our equation: the analysis still applies. Any solution is either odd, or if it’s even then we can cancel powers of 2 from both sides and obtain an odd solution. If we figure out the odd solutions, we’re done. Notice, now, that if x and y are both odd then x 2 + 1 and y 2 + 1 are both even, which means that x y 2 + 1 and y x 2 + 1 are both perfect squares. We now have a power of 2 , namely 2 z , expressed as the sum of two squares – and there are very few ways to do that. In fact, the only ways of writing 2 z as the sum of two squares are 2 z = 0 + 2 z , which only works when z is even, and 2 z = 2 z − 1 + 2 z − 1 , which only works when z is odd. That’s an immediate consequence of Jacobi’s two-square theorem, and I think it should be possible to prove it directly, without too much preparation, but I didn’t try to do so. It’s a fairly familiar fact that powers of 2 are never an “interesting” sum of squares. With that, we’re done: the only odd solution is 1 + 1 = 2 , because any larger A , B with A = B would be divisible by an odd prime. Therefore the only solutions of the original equation are x = y = 2 k , z = 2 2 k + 2 . (…)

Is there a general formula to solve the equation:
a

where n can be any natural number?
Answer: I could defend each of the answers “yes”, “no” and “we don’t know”. Let’s start with the “no”. Let’s take a very special case of your question, like 2 x 5 − 10 x + 5 = 0 . This equation defines 5 complex numbers which are its roots; but what are they? Can we express them in some kind of “formula”? We know that we can’t express them with radicals, the way we do with equations of degree n = 2 , 3 , 4 . Galois theory precisely shows that (the Galois group of this particular polynomial is the non-solvable group S 5 ). So that’s a first-degree “no” answer to the question. But what about other expressions? Trig functions, logs, etc.? In the paper What is a closed-form number, Tim Chow uses the very same polynomial equation as an example. He then proves that, under the well-known Schanuel conjecture, the roots of this equation (or any other polynomial equation with non-solvable Galois group) are not EL-numbers, which means they cannot be expressed with any of the familiar elementary functions (logs, exponents, trig functions, roots and any combination thereof.) So that’s a second-degree “no” answer: the roots of such equations aren’t EL numbers, which means that they cannot be expressed with formulas consisting of logs, exponents, sines, cosines, arctangents and other familiar functions. Even specific polynomial equations don’t have roots that are expressible in this way, let alone a general formula. But, to be fair, Chow’s result rests on a big, unproven conjecture. It’s possible (though extremely unlikely) that the conjecture is false and that somehow, miraculously, there’s some EL expression for the roots of polynomial equations. So, in that sense, and sticking with EL numbers as the correct universe of “formulas”, the precise answer is “we don’t know”. Finally, the answer may reasonably be “yes” if you allow more flexibility in the concept of “formula”. For example, polynomial equations of degree n = 5 can be solved with the Bring radical, and higher-degree polynomials can be handled with other fancy functions. From a different perspective, polynomial equations with rational coefficients can be solved efficiently with methods such as Newton-Raphson. Those are iterative in nature, and I often see people object to them because they don’t offer a “closed” expression. But you may want to ask yourself, why would you accept a formula such as tan ( log ( 5 ) ) as a solution? What does this expression do for you that Newton-Raphson does not? Sure, we’re familiar with those functions and may feel we “get” them, but computing the value of such an expression is exactly the same kind of iterative procedure as Newton-Raphson: you can iterate and produce an approximation at any desired accuracy. From this perspective, the roots of polynomial equations with rational coefficients are computable numbers, and it’s reasonable to equate computability with “having a formula”, even if the formula isn’t as succinct and friendly as the quadratic formula. Answer: This is the kind of problem that suits a rather narrow interval of mathematical maturity. Too early it is useless, and too late it’s a bit too easy. For students who are already comfortable with logarithms and derivatives this is not a bad exercise, but it’s fairly easy. Many such students are already familiar with the general result (for numbers above 3 , or more precisely above e , the larger between a b and b a is the one with the larger exponent and smaller base). So I think this question is meant to be tackled without logarithms and derivatives and sealing wax and other fancy stuff. I tested my ability to do this in my head while biking home from work, and it worked, I think. Here’s how. First of all, n = 10 is easy: we have equality. What happens when we move one step up, to n = 11 ? The left side was 10 10 and now it’s 10 11 which is exactly 10 times larger. What about the right side? It was 10 10 and now it’s 11 10 , so it grew by a factor of… every 10 became 11 , so a factor of 1.1 , and this happens 10 times so the right side grew by a factor of 1.1 10 . Is 1.1 10 more than or less than 10 ? Again, no fancy stuff (forget what you know about e ). Let’s just square a few times. 1.1 2 is certainly less than 1.5 , so 1.1 4 is certainly less than 2.5 , so 1.1 8 is certainly less than 7 , and multiplying that by 1.1 twice is like 7.7 and then, whatever, less than 9 . So yeah, 10 > 1.1 10 and the left side, 10 n , beats n 10 handily at n = 11 . And now the key part: we’re done with numbers n above 10 . They are all out. Why? Because next time we move up, from 11 to 12 , the left side will once again grow by a factor of 10 , and the right side will grow by, instead of ( 11 / 10 ) 10 , by ( 12 / 11 ) 10 , and this is a smaller factor. Right? 12 / 11 is 1 plus 1 / 11 , which is less than 1 plus 1 / 10 . And so on and so forth: when we move from n to n + 1 , the expression 10 n gets multiplied by 10 and the expression n 10 gets multiplied by ( 1 + 1 / n ) 10 which is less than 1.1 10 , and we’ve already established that this is less than 10 . So, 10 n is greater than n 10 when n > 10 . What about when n < 10 ? This is not a huge deal because there are only 9 numbers to check, and some of them are really easy. There are other ways of handling n = 9 , for instance with the binomial theorem (try it). And I’m sorry about n = 7 . See if you can do it with the same kind of simple comparisons. So the answer is, the n 's which make 10 n ≤ n 10 are n = 2 , 3 , … , 10 , and there are 9 such numbers. (…)

Question: Suppose that you have a black box that solves the halting problem: when queried with M and x, the black box tells you whether M(x) halts or not. Assuming this, give an algorithm (using the black box 1 time) that solves Collatz Conjecture?
Answer: You can’t do that. You can write a simple program L which requires no input, and searches for closed loops under the Collatz map. Keep a set of Collatz paths and, at each iteration, advance all paths one step forward, and start a new path at the smallest integer not yet visited. Stop when you identify a closed loop that’s not 1 , 4 , 2 , 1 . Feed L to the halting oracle. If the oracle says L halts, we know that the Collatz conjecture is false: there’s a closed loop other than the trivial one. If the oracle says the program never halts, we know that there isn’t… …but that doesn’t solve Collatz. We still don’t know if there’s an infinite path: a starting value which, upon iterating the Collatz map, keep growing forever, never looping. Determining if there is or isn’t such an infinite path is not something you can solve with a mere halting oracle. The reason is that the assertion that there’s no such infinite path sits at the second level of the arithmetic hierarchy, not the first. For each starting value, you can use an oracle to determine if the path starting at that value does or doesn’t lead to a loop, but you can’t ask an oracle if all of these programs halt: you need a second-level oracle which can determine if a program that calls a halting oracle ever halts. In terms of the arithmetic hierarchy, we are at Σ 2 . In terms of the Turing hierarchy, we are at 0 ′′ rather than merely 0 ′ . It is possible, of course, that there is a proof of the Collatz conjecture, in which case we can solve it with no oracles at all. It’s also possible that someone will present a Σ 1 sentence that’s equivalent to the Collatz conjecture, and at that point we could use a halting oracle to resolve it. But as things stand now, you can’t settle Collatz with an oracle for the halting problem. Added later: the question is phrased like an exercise from a textbook or course. If that’s the case, that source is misguided. The task is not feasible, and the source is of somewhat suspect quality. If I had to guess the root of the misunderstanding, it may be lack of clarity of what “the halting problem” is, exactly. An oracle for the halting problem is supposed to answer correctly the halting question for ordinary programs: Turing machines. It’s not supposed to solve the halting question for programs which themselves have the ability to consult with halting oracles. That’s the whole point of the Turing Jump. The question doesn’t specify what “M” is, exactly. The correct interpretation is that M is a Turing machine, and that’s probably why it’s called “M”, and if so, that’s fine, but the question is wrong. If M is somehow supposed to represent programs with access to a halting oracle, then the question is solvable, but that’s not the correct meaning of the term “black box that solves the halting problem”. Nicolò Bonacorsi, where’s the question taken from? (…)

Answer: That’s a very nice question. Thanks to m = n = 1 , 2 has the same color as 3 . That’s a good start, but how do we show that they have the same color as 4 ? Trying other small values of m , n doesn’t seem to lead us back to 4 . So…? Oh but you see, 3 has the same color as 6 (why?), which has the same color as 19 (why?), which has the same color as 206 (see why?), and then 17 , 146 , 13 , 86 , 11 and finally 4 . So yeah, 4 must carry the same color as 2 and 3 , but the chaotic path we needed to follow to see this is a bit disheartening. What to do? When you look at that path, you can’t miss the fact that the numbers zig-zag between small and large. This isn’t at all surprising: you have some small m , n and they let you connect m + n (small) to m 2 + n 2 + 1 (much larger), and what happens then is that this number m 2 + n 2 + 1 happens to have another representation as M 2 + N 2 + 1 , which leads you back to M + N , roughly the same size as m + n . For example, 13 → 86 because 13 = 6 + 7 and 6 2 + 7 2 + 1 = 86 , but also 9 2 + 2 2 + 1 = 86 and that gives us 86 → 9 + 2 = 11 . In two hops we’ve connected 11 and 13 , which seems much more useful than connecting 13 to 86 . (When I say “connecting” I just mean that these two numbers must be colored in the same color, as per the specification of the question. The question here is really about proving that the implied graph is connected.) The key here wasn’t the number 86 , it was the number 85 : it’s the sum of two squares in two different ways, just like Ramanujan’s 1729 but with squares instead of cubes. So my idea was to manufacture lots of numbers that are sums of squares in two different ways, and from that infer lots of nearby connections like 11 ↔ 13 , and from that conclude that all the integers > 1 are eventually connected. That turned out to be easier said than done. There was one thing the confused me briefly: if all we’re doing is hopping from m + n to M + N whenever m 2 + n 2 = M 2 + N 2 , why the + 1 ? As far as we’re concerned it doesn’t seem to matter at all… but I quickly realized that if the question had m 2 + n 2 instead of m 2 + n 2 + 1 , the conclusion would certainly be false: even numbers and odd numbers would never get connected. The + 1 is what let us connect 2 to 3 , and that explains why it’s there. Right. So how do we find many instance of m 2 + n 2 = M 2 + N 2 ? I thought I knew the answer to that, and it turned out that I was not as learned as I thought I was. My first approach was to rewrite this as m 2 − M 2 = N 2 − n 2 , so ( m − M ) ( m + M ) = ( N − n ) ( N + n ) , and that’s just some number which affords two factorizations in which the factors have the same parity. Any two numbers of the same parity can be written as X − x and X + x . So yes, sure, there are many composite numbers and most of them can be expressed in a few different ways like that, but it was hard to put enough structure on this to obtain a nice family of connections. (That was a mistake; I just didn’t look at it the right way. But I needed a jolt from a different direction to see this). The jolt came when I arranged a few square-pairs and noticed that they follow a pattern. The first observation, for some odd reason, was this: ( x + 3 ) 2 + ( 3 x − 1 ) 2 = ( x − 3 ) 2 + ( 3 x + 1 ) 2 Once you see this, it’s hard to unsee it: this is pretty darn obvious. The square terms on both sides are the same, the constant terms on both sides are the same, and the linear terms on both sides are missing. Of course that’s true. It’s a simple polynomial identity, but I have to admit I never noticed the existence of such simple polynomial identities. Now I know. I like this question for teaching me that. This observation means, for our question, that all numbers of the form ( x + 3 ) + ( 3 x − 1 ) = 4 x + 2 are connected (in two hops) to ( x − 3 ) + ( 3 x + 1 ) = 4 x − 2 , as soon as x ≥ 4 (because otherwise x − 3 isn’t a positive integer, and the question only allows m , n to be positive integers.) I then generalized this in an obvious way: ( a x + b ) 2 + ( b x − a ) 2 = ( a x − b ) 2 + ( b x + a ) 2 (1) for any positive integers a , b you like. Now take, for example, a = 1 , b = 2 to see ( x + 2 ) 2 + ( 2 x − 1 ) 2 = ( x − 2 ) 2 + ( 2 x + 1 ) 2 which lets us connect 3 x − 1 to 3 x + 1 whenever x ≥ 3 is an integer. Nice! We now have two connecting rules with different multipliers, which seems to make our colors very restricted. I figured that if I collected enough of these I’d be done. That’s right, and I’ll show how, but I have this nagging feeling that there’s a much more elegant way to do this that I’m completely missing. Whatever. I’m never as smart as I think I am. Now, I said that the composite numbers view could work and I just missed it. In fact, if you rearrange the identity (1) as a difference of squares and then replace X 2 − x 2 with ( X + x ) ( X − x ) , you’ll see that it is simply 2 a x ⋅ 2 b = 2 b x ⋅ 2 a , so duh. Of course that’s true, and the only thing I should have done is look at simple factorizations such as 4 a b = 4 b a and throw a parameter x inside, to get a whole family of sum-of-squares identities. Here’s another example: from 2 x ⋅ 12 = 4 x ⋅ 6 we can infer ( x + 6 ) 2 − ( x − 6 ) 2 = ( 2 x + 3 ) 2 − ( 2 x − 3 ) 2 , another identity which seems obvious in hindsight, and it lets us assert that the numbers 3 x + 3 and 3 x − 3 are connected. That’s genuinely different from 3 x + 1 and 3 x − 1 . So far we’ve got the following “rules”, each implying that various types of numbers are connected, so they must have the same color: I should say something about the last one: it actually follows directly from the conditions of the question, setting m = x and n = 1 . It’s much simpler to derive than the other three, and you may wonder why I didn’t emphasize more rules like that. Their weakness is that they connect something linear to something quadratic, which is a lot less helpful in general. But it’s still convenient to have it at our disposal, as we’ll see in a minute. So now, back to the original problem. Assume that 2 is colored pink, and we need to show that all numbers must be colored pink as well. Our strategy is simple: Part 1 just requires a bit of patience. We already know that 2 , 3 , 4 are pink, and 3 ↔ 6 by D. Since 4 = 2 + 2 we also have 4 ↔ 9 , and by D again 9 ↔ 66 . Using B several times we can drop from 66 to 42 , and then C to 38 and D to 7 . From 42 we can also take another two B’s to 18 and a D to 5 . Finally 6 to 27 (D) to 51 (Bs) to 8 , and using A to 10 . We have all the numbers from 2 to 10 pink, and you can easily get up to 30 yourself as an exercise. We can easily get all even numbers now: suppose that Z is the smallest even non-pink number. It must be > 30 , and consider what it can be mod 12 : It can’t be 0 or 6 because if it is then rule B shows it has the same color as Z − 6 which is known to be pink. It can’t be 2 or 10 mod 12 because C shows it has the same color as Z − 4 , nor 4 mod 12 because rule A shows it has the same color as Z − 2 . Finally, 8 mod 12 is solved by moving forward to 10 using A, and then back down using C again. All even numbers are pink. That’s part 2 of the plan. What about odd numbers? Easy: rule D. Right? So all numbers are pink and we’re done. ■ Again, I’m sure there’s a more elegant way, but this works, and I learned something which is always excellent. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: If maths teachers desperately want their students to feel mathematics matters in the 'real' world, how come they keep giving them quadratic equations to solve that can be factorised nicely over the integers?
Answer: As far as I can tell, math (or maths) teachers wish to teach students whatever materials are mandated by the local curricula. Many of them also care about a deeper understanding, or having fun, or talking about the history, or the people, or something else. Sometimes they are “desperate”. More often they aren’t that at all. Some teaches do like showing how math matters, whether it’s their own personal drive or an actual part of the local curriculum. You seem to believe that giving exercises with nicely factorizing quadratics is contrary to that mission. I can’t imagine why you’d think that. We teach quadratic equations not because solving quadratic equations is important for someone’s peculiar idea of a “real world”. What real world demands that you solve quadratic equations? I mean, sure, they may pop up here and there, but never for most people, and a little bit for a few people whose work involves lots of math, of which quadratics may take up some 0.001%. We teach quadratic equations because they are a useful instance of a well-defined problem that can be solved algorithmically, yet requires some pattern matching, some understanding of algebra, facility with manipulating expressions, and other basic skills that enrich young minds in a variety of ways. There’s nothing more “real worldy” about 2.1 x 2 − 18.55 x + 17.29 = 0 as opposed to x 2 − 5 x + 6 = 0 . They are both fine equations, and they differ in the details of solving them. There really is no need to disallow the latter in favor of the former’s “real world credentials”. It’s a non-issue. That’s not the point. (I happen to think that there’s value in having students more often work through problem sets with no clean solutions. But that’s not because I worry about their readiness to whatever real world awaits them.) (…)

Question: Is it indeed true that Princeton have a better math department than Harvard does? If so, then why does Harvard have far more Putnam Competition titles?
Answer: There’s no objective sense in which one math department is “better” than another; research, teaching, field focus and culture are all multi-dimensional and impossible to quantify in a meaningfully objective sense. (There’s no need to point out that the math department at prominent university X is likely “better” in most dimensions than that of a tiny college in some remote region of the world. I understand that. But putting the departments of strong research universities on a linear scale is truly meaningless, despite what the editors of US News would have you believe.) And of all the ways to gauge the quality or strength or suitability of a math department to your needs, counting Putnam titles is particularly pointless. Some universities happen to have faculty members who put a lot of effort into the Putnam, and a strong tradition of taking it very seriously; some universities don’t. MIT is almost ridiculously successful at it, but that doesn’t mean that its math department is 20x better than all other math departments combined. It just means that MIT puts significant emphasis on competition math, and that probably affects its applicant pool, acceptance criteria, efforts in preparing the team and maybe a few other factors. It doesn’t mean that its faculty has “better” researchers, or teachers, or human beings. (None of this is meant to criticize Yufei or the MIT Putnam contestants. They’re brilliant and awesome. I just wish to clarify that the question, as phrased, makes little sense. Also, to allay concerns that I’m talking out of some kind of spite or jealousy, my alma mater is outside the US so it doesn’t participate in the Putnam, and my math-majoring kid happened to have chosen a school with stellar recent Putnam record, and he chose it for completely different reasons. Really, it’s not that.) (…)

Question: If prime numbers thin out tremendously the higher you go, but even numbers remain every other number til infinity, how can the Binary Goldbach Conjecture possibly be true? Aren't there too few prime pairs to go around?
Answer: Prime numbers don’t thin out “tremendously”. They thin out gently and quietly. Suppose that the density of primes was always 1%. Always. Meaning, roughly every 100th number was prime. In that case you would say that the primes don’t thin out at all. Right? Sure, they are pretty sparse, but their sparseness never drops one bit – it’s steady, forever. This isn’t actually the case, of course. The density of primes eventually drops below 1%. But do you know how far you have to go until this happens? Up until around 26881171418161354484126255515800135873600000 , give or take. In contrast, the sequence 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 of powers of 2 drops below 1% right around 100 . This sequence thins out geometrically, which you may call “tremendously” if you like. The primes do nothing even close to that. They thin out… but very, very, very slowly. And in fact, as Nathan showed, this gentle thinning does the exact opposite of what you’re proposing: it makes the Goldbach Conjecture fantastically likely. Once you’ve checked GC for the first, oh, I don’t know, 100,000 numbers, you can virtually stop checking. Larger numbers are ridiculously unlikely to fail the GC conjecture. (…)

Question: Let α and ω be 2 circles such that ω goes through the center of α. ω intersects α at A and B. Let P be any point on the circumference ω. The lines PA and PB intersects α again at E and F respectively. How to prove that AB = EF?
Answer: Start with a simpler situation, with just one circle. We have a circle with center O , a point P not on the circle, and two lines from P such that P O is their angle bisector. Then A E = F B . You can prove this by sheer symmetry: the whole diagram is symmetric around the line P O . Flip it around and the line segments A E and F B map onto each other. Now here’s the situation described in the question: The point P now lies on a circle which passes through O . But this precisely ensures that P O bisects the angle between P A and P B , because the angles ∠ B P O and ∠ A P O subtend congruent arcs. (Proof, again, by symmetry, this time around the line Q O ). By the previous observation, A E = F B and we are done. ■ (…)

Question: Let p, q and r be prime numbers, and n > 0, such that all belong to Z and p^n + q^n = r^2. How can I demonstrate that n most be 1?
Answer: First, let’s see what happens when n is even. If the primes p , q are both odd then p n ≡ q n ≡ 1 ( mod 4 ) , so the sum p n + q n is 2 mod 4 and cannot be a perfect square. Therefore one of p , q , let’s say q , satisfies q = 2 , and for now let’s consider p odd. We have p n + 2 n = r 2 . We may write n = 2 m (since n is even) and so p 2 m = r 2 − ( 2 m ) 2 = ( r − 2 m ) ( r + 2 m ) If r − 2 m > 1 then it’s divisible by some prime, and the only possible prime is p , so p divides both r − 2 m and r + 2 m and therefore also their difference 2 m + 1 which is impossible. So we must have r = 2 m + 1 , and p 2 m = 2 m + 1 + 1 . This is easy to rule out as p > 2 and either m = 1 (doesn’t work) or 2 m > m + 1 and the LHS is larger than the RHS. Finally, we should check the case p = q = 2 . Then p n + q n = 2 n + 1 = r 2 and r can’t be prime. So n can’t be even. If n is odd then the polynomial X n + Y n is divisible by X + Y , so p n + q n is divisible by p + q . Assuming n > 1 , p + q is a proper divisor of p n + q n = r 2 , but r is prime so we must have p + q = r . Now we have p n + q n = ( p + q ) 2 . Forget primes for a moment and consider the equation in real variables x n + y n = ( x + y ) 2 with n ≥ 3 . For any fixed value of the sum x + y = 2 t , x n + y n is minimized when x = y = t , and as soon as t > 2 we have t n + t n > ( 2 t ) 2 and there can be no equality. So x n + y n = ( x + y ) 2 can only be solved if x + y ≤ 4 , and going back to our primes this means p = q = 2 and then r = 4 isn’t a prime. So n can’t be odd and ≥ 3 either, and the only remaining option is n = 1 . ■ The case n = 1 is more subtle. We can obviously have p = q = r = 2 , but if r > 2 then it must be odd which means that q = 2 . We’re now looking at p + 2 = r 2 , or in other words we’re looking for prime numbers r such that r 2 − 2 is also prime. There are many such primes (over 1,500 with r < 10 5 ), and it’s not known if there are infinitely many. Therefore the equation p n + q n = r 2 is actually very subtle when n = 1 . (…)

Question: Do there exist finitely generated groups that have an infinite minimal generating set?
Answer: Nice question. The answer is no. First, to eliminate any confusion: a minimal generating set doesn’t mean a generating set with the smallest possible cardinality. It means a generating set for which any proper subset is no longer a generating set. In other words, it’s a generating set that has no redundancy: removing any element makes the set no longer generate the whole group. For example, in the additive group Z of integers, { 1 } is a generating set that’s obviously minimal, but { 2 , 3 } is also a minimal generating set, as is { 6 , 10 , 15 } . In fact (exercise), there are minimal generating sets with k elements, for any k ∈ N > 0 . However, Z does not possess an infinite minimal generating set, not does any other finitely-generated group. To see this, let G be a finitely-generated group, S a finite generating set of G , and X an infinite generating set. For every s ∈ S we can pick a subset X s ⊂ X such that s ∈ ⟨ X s ⟩ : this is possible because ⟨ X ⟩ = G . The key point is that X s can be taken to be finite: the element s can be expressed as a product of the elements of X and their inverses, and any such expression is, by definition, finite. So s already belongs to ⟨ X s ⟩ for some finite set X s . Now, the union ⋃ s ∈ S X s ⊂ X is finite, and it generates S , so it generates G . Therefore X , the infinite generating set, isn’t minimal: it has a finite generating subset. ■ (…)

Question: After primality test of the first 40 odd numbers in a range (10^100000000+1)-(10^100000000+99), only 8 numbers remained indivisible. Even if it's being an amateur, is this still worth nothing?
Answer: Hello, Andrew Mwaba! Please note that your Quora bio currently reads “Upcoming scientist with five useful unpunished ideas”. I think you mean “unpublished”. It appears you’re exploring the divisibility of numbers N + k for N = 10 10 8 and 1 ≤ k < 100 . Perhaps your goal is to find a new prime record? Please don’t. This is not a reasonable undertaking by any stretch of the imagination. About 1 in 200,000,000 numbers in this range is prime. You’re exploring 100 such numbers. Those aren’t great odds, but the real problem is that even if by some miracle one of those numbers happens to be prime, there is no way current technology can prove that. I’m serious: no way. You seem to have tested those numbers for divisibility by small primes. Indeed, most of them are found to be divisible by very small primes; for example, N + 3 is divisible by 7 . You say that 8 numbers remained indivisible, so I’m guessing you searched for primes through 500 or so; that does indeed leaves N + k indivisible for k ∈ { 1 , 19 , 37 , 63 , 69 , 93 , 97 , 99 } . However, if you extend your small prime search a bit further, you should be left with just 2 candidates ( 69 and 93 ). For example: This took only a few minutes to program and run. But all of this is besides the point: this is not a useful way of detecting primes, and the sheer observation that many of those numbers are divisible by small primes is neither interesting nor useful. If you’re interested in such things, there’s much to learn and much to enjoy, but the approach you’re taking won’t lead you to a deeper understanding or any sort of worthy achievement. Please don’t. Name: Alon Amit
Question: Is it mathematically kosher to prove that the sum of the reciprocals of the prime numbers diverges by invoking the Prime Number Theorem, whereby the nth prime ~ n*log(n), and then doing a simple integration of d (log(u)) /log(u) from 1 to infinity?
Answer: Kinda yes, but actually no. The smaller issue is that the PNT doesn’t tell you that the n th prime is n log ( n ) , it just says that it is roughly that, in a sense that can be made precise. So you can’t just glibly replace p n by n log ( n ) in a computation. This can be handled by using appropriate upper bounds (e.g. Dusart’s bound), so it’s not a huge issue, and in many contexts you can totally get away with it even in its imprecise form. The bigger problem, however, is that this is essentially a circular argument. You’re using an advanced result, the PNT, to “prove” something that is itself a tiny step in the proof of the PNT. Or, at least, potentially so. I mean, it’s possible to write down a complete proof of the PNT without ever uttering the words “the series of prime reciprocals diverges”, but I don’t think it’s possible to write down such a proof without proving at some (early) point something stronger or essentially equivalent. There are, by now, many proofs of the PNT, and I’m sure it’s technically possible to start from first principles and write down an intricate proof of the divergence of ∑ 1 / p ∑ by first proving the full PNT in some way, then showing something like Dusart’s inequality, and eventually concluding the divergence of prime reciprocals. But this makes little logical sense. Many PNT proofs start by analyzing the behavior of ζ ( s ) near the pole s = 1 . The prime reciprocals sum can be understood as the value at s = 1 of the prime zeta function, which in this region is easily seen to be essentially the log of the usual Riemann zeta function. That’s all you need, and it would be bizarre to proceed all the way to the PNT just to go back and prove something you could have proven in line 5. At any rate, formally, if you wish to invoke Theorem T in order to prove fact F, you must make sure that you have a proof of theorem T which doesn’t in any way rely on fact F at any point. Otherwise, you’ve achieved nothing. This can probably be done here, but it’s hard to make sure, and it certainly doesn’t make sense. If anything, I would use Chebyshev’s much simpler and earlier results on the prime counting function to prove something like that. It’s still a much bigger hammer than necessary, but at least it’s not a nuclear weapon. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question:
What is the largest possible radius of a circle contained in a
4
-dimensional hypercube of side length
1
?
Answer: Ah, yes, B-3 from the 2008 Putnam competition. Here’s how I (think I) approached it (to be clear: offline, not during the competition. I expect it took me something like 2 weeks of thinking on and off to solve it.) We’re in R 4 , and the nicest hypercube to work with is H = { v | − 1 ≤ v 1 , v 2 , v 3 , v 4 ≤ 1 } : the collection of 4 -vectors whose coordinates are all between − 1 and 1 . This hypercube has side length 2 , but never mind: we just need to remember to rescale our answer by a factor of 2 . This choice is just nicer because there are no fractions and the center of the cube is at the origin. A circle in R n , for any n , looks like this: there’s a center O , and some 2 -dimensional plane passing through O , and the circle is the set of vectors on that plane whose distance from O is some fixed radius r . We can find two perpendicular vectors u , v of length r on that plane (just choose an orthonormal basis and rescale it by r ), and then the circle is just the set of points O + u cos θ + v sin θ for 0 ≤ θ < 2 π . Such a circle in R 4 lies inside of H if all of these vectors have coordinates between − 1 and 1 . We may assume that the center O has non-negative coordinates (there’s no difference between this or that “octant” of the cube.) If our circle is best possible, some coordinate of O + u cos θ + v sin θ is ± 1 ; but if it’s − 1 , changing θ to − θ would make it 1 or more, because O contributes something positive (or 0 ). Therefore, zeroing out each coordinate of O keeps such a circle neatly inside H , and we might as well assume O = 0 . The optimal circle is centered at the origin, which make perfect intuitive sense. So now we just have two vectors u and v , and for each index 1 ≤ i ≤ 4 and any angle θ we have | u i cos θ + v i sin θ | ≤ 1 . In particular, this must be true for the angle θ whose cosine is u i / ( u 2 i + v 2 i ) and whose sine is v i / ( u 2 i + v 2 i ) (this is just the angle with tan θ = v i / u i ). From this particular θ we conclude that u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 . Suppose, conversely, that u , v are two orthogonal, equal-length vectors in R 4 satisfying the four inequalities u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 . For any angle θ and any i , consider the 2-d vectors x = ( u i , v i ) and y = ( cos θ , sin θ ) . By Cauchy-Schwartz, | u i cos θ + v i sin θ | 2 = | x ⋅ y | 2 ≤ ⟨ x , x ⟩ ⟨ y , y ⟩ = u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 so, indeed, | u i cos θ + v i sin θ | ≤ 1 and the circle defined by these vectors doesn’t breach the hypercube. Conclusion: the circles contained in H are parametrized precisely by pairs of vectors u , v which are orthogonal of equal length and satisfy u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 for i = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , and such a pair determines a circle of radius r with r 2 = u 2 1 + u 2 2 + u 2 3 + u 2 4 = v 2 1 + v 2 2 + v 2 3 + v 2 4 . But now, adding these equations up we find that 2 r 2 = u 2 1 + v 2 1 + u 2 2 + v 2 2 + u 2 3 + v 2 3 + u 2 4 + v 2 4 ≤ 4 or r 2 ≤ 2 , or r ≤ √ 2 , and we have an upper bound: any circle in H has radius not greater than √ 2 . Furthermore, it’s easy to find a suitable circle of just such a radius: take u = ( 1 , 1 , 0 , 0 ) and v = ( 0 , 0 , 1 , 1 ) . Those are orthogonal vectors, of the same length √ 2 , and they satisfy u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 for i = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . So the largest circle in H has radius √ 2 , and the largest circle in a hypercube of edge-length 1 has radius √ 2 / 2 . ■ (…)

Question: How can you prove that the Bruijn digraph B (d, n) is an Eulerian and Hamiltonian?
Answer: De Bruijn graphs are Eulerian because all vertices obviously have equal in-deg and out-deg, and they are also obviously strongly connected (you can reach any given string from any other given string by successive shifts and insertions of new characters). Question: Why do we have several geometries (Euclidean, Spherical, Non-Euclidean…) but only one arithmetic? Why everything can be described with same arithmetic but requires different geometries?
Answer: Both “Arithmetic” and “Geometry” are not formally defined terms. If you take a very broad view of what counts as “Geometry” and an extremely narrow view of what counts as “Arithmetic” then, sure, you could find many geometries and a single arithmetic, but this is merely a reflection of the choice of interpretation of these particular terms. To describe “everything” we need many, many more than “several” geometries, and many, many more than a single arithmetical structure. The ancient Euclidean geometry evolved into a small part of what is now called synthetic geometry, which itself is just a small part of geometry - differential geometry, algebraic geometry, Riemannian geometry, and many other types of geometry are being studied nowadays, each offering infinitely many spaces and structures to explore. Similarly, school arithmetic is now a tiny part of what can variably be described as Number Theory (and specifically Algebraic Number Theory), Abstract Algebra, Ring Theory, Field Theory and various other overlapping domains. Both Geometry and Arithmetic, in a broad sense, are huge parts of modern mathematics, and exist in infinitely many different shapes and forms. (…)

Question: Is n^3 + 2 square free for all positive integers, n?
Answer: Not at all. You can see that the answer is no without computing anything, with some understanding of how polynomials behave mod m . Except under unusual circumstances (when the derivative vanishes mod p ), once a polynomial has a root mod a prime p it also has roots mod any power of p . For example, our polynomial here is going to behave strangely mod 3 , so let’s skip that. Looking at n = 2 we find 2 3 + 2 = 10 which is divisible by 5 , so we have a root mod 5 and automatically we know there’ll be a root mod 25 , or in other words at some point 25 will divide n 3 + 2 . This, indeed, happens with n = 2 + 4 ⋅ 5 = 22 , but there’s no need to compute that. We already know it’s going to happen. The same behavior will be observed with any polynomial. (…)

Question: Is it true that there are math Olympiad problems that people with PhDs in mathematics and related fields struggle with?
Answer: Of course. That’s the point of them being math Olympiad problems: they are very challenging. Perhaps the assumption is that a challenging problem for a high school student must be a walk in the park for a graduate student, or a Ph.D. holder, or a mathematician in an academic position. This isn’t so. Problem solving is an important part of math research, but it’s not quite the same kind as Olympiad problem solving, and earning a Ph.D. in math takes skills and dedication of a different character. Some mathematicians enjoy Olympiad-style problem solving and can handle many Olympiad problems faster than you or me, but many don’t, and even the best of them may not be able to earn top scores at a recent IMO. The kids who participate at the IMO are deeply immersed in this style of problems, they are well trained, and they have just the right type of smarts for this challenge: creative structuring of strategies, blazing fast assessment of different ideas and directions to pursue, tenacity, imagination and a keen sense of abstract analogies. All of these things are useful for math research in general, but Ph.D. students don’t have to be as crazy athletic at them as the Olympiad kids are. By way of analogy, think how well most professional sportspeople – say, NBA players – would do at the majority of summer Olympics events – say, artistic gymnastics. (…)
